title: Chapter 2: LLMs, Prompts, Tokens, and APIs Without Confusion
content:
Chapter 2: LLMs, Prompts, Tokens, and APIs Without Confusion

Opening Hook: The Model Is Not the App

In Chapter 1, you built your first Python AI assistant: a code explainer.

That project did something powerful.

It took Python code as input, sent a carefully written prompt to an AI model, and returned a useful explanation.

But there was one problem.

The model-calling code was inside the project itself.

That is fine for your first project.

But if you keep copying API code into every new app, your projects will quickly become messy.

In this chapter, you will fix that.

You will build a reusable Python class called LLMClient.

This client will become the foundation for later projects.

Instead of rewriting API logic again and again, you will use one clean interface:

response = client.complete(
system="You are a helpful assistant.",
user="Explain Python lists."
)

That is much better.

This chapter also clears up the confusing terms people use when talking about AI apps:

  • LLMs
  • Prompts
  • Tokens
  • Context
  • APIs
  • Models
  • Temperature
  • Cost
  • Latency

You do not need to become a machine learning researcher to build useful AI apps.

But you do need to understand these practical ideas.

By the end of this chapter, you will have a reusable LLM client that you can use throughout the rest of the book.

What You Will Learn

By the end of this chapter, you will understand:

  • What an LLM is at a practical level
  • What prompts are
  • What system and user instructions do
  • What tokens are
  • Why context length matters
  • What an API is
  • How model selection affects quality, speed, and cost
  • What temperature means
  • How to avoid hardcoding secrets
  • How to build a reusable LLM client in Python
  • How to test non-API logic without spending credits
  • How to design code that can be adapted to different AI providers

Why This Chapter Matters

Most beginner AI apps fail for one of three reasons.

Reason 1: API Code Is Repeated Everywhere

Beginners often copy the same API setup into every file.

That creates duplication.

When the API changes, they must update many files.

A reusable client solves this.

Reason 2: Prompts Are Scattered Through the Code

If prompts are hidden in random functions, the app becomes hard to improve.

A cleaner structure separates:

API client
prompt templates
app logic
tests

Reason 3: Cost and Errors Are Ignored

AI apps can fail because:

  • API keys are missing
  • Inputs are too long
  • Model names are wrong
  • Network calls fail
  • Outputs are too expensive
  • Prompts are unclear
  • The app calls the model unnecessarily

This chapter introduces habits that prevent those problems.

2.1 What Is an LLM?

LLM stands for Large Language Model.

At a practical level, an LLM is a model that accepts input text and generates output text.

You send:

Explain what a Python dictionary is.

The model returns something like:

A Python dictionary stores data as key-value pairs.

An LLM can help with:

  • Explanation
  • Summarization
  • Rewriting
  • Classification
  • Question answering
  • Code assistance
  • Planning
  • Drafting
  • Reasoning over provided context

But an LLM is not your full application.

An LLM is one part of your application.

Your Python code still needs to handle:

  • User input
  • Files
  • API keys
  • Prompt construction
  • Tool calls
  • Memory
  • Retrieval
  • Validation
  • Error handling
  • Display
  • Deployment

A useful AI app is built around the model.

2.2 What Is a Prompt?

A prompt is the instruction you send to the model.

Simple prompt:

Explain Python lists.

Better prompt:

Explain Python lists for a beginner.
Use one short example.
Avoid advanced jargon.

Even better prompt:

You are a friendly Python tutor.

Explain Python lists for a beginner.

Return:
1. Short definition
2. Simple example
3. Common mistake
4. Beginner-friendly summary

The third prompt is better because it gives:

  • Role
  • Audience
  • Task
  • Format
  • Constraints

Good prompts are not magic words.

They are clear instructions.

2.3 System Instructions and User Requests

In many AI apps, you separate instructions into two layers.

System Instruction

The system instruction defines the assistant’s behavior.

Example:

You are a helpful Python tutor.
Be clear, accurate, and beginner-friendly.
Do not invent facts.

User Request

The user request contains what the user wants right now.

Example:

Explain the difference between a list and a tuple.

Together, they form the full model input.

System:
You are a helpful Python tutor.

User:
Explain the difference between a list and a tuple.

This separation helps you keep the assistant consistent while allowing the user request to change.

2.4 What Are Tokens?

A token is a small piece of text processed by the model.

A token may be:

  • A word
  • Part of a word
  • Punctuation
  • Whitespace
  • A symbol

For practical beginner purposes, you can think:

More text means more tokens.

Tokens matter because they affect:

  • Cost
  • Speed
  • Context length
  • How much information fits in one request

A short prompt costs less and runs faster than a very long prompt.

A RAG app that sends 20 pages of context every time will usually cost more than one that sends only the most relevant chunks.

This is why retrieval, chunking, and prompt design matter.

2.5 What Is Context Length?

Context length means how much information the model can consider in one request.

This includes:

System instructions
+ user message
+ conversation history
+ retrieved documents
+ tool results
+ any other prompt text

If you send too much information, you may hit limits or increase cost.

Even when a model supports a long context window, sending everything is not always wise.

Better practice:

Send only what is useful for the task.

That is why RAG is important.

Instead of sending an entire document, a RAG app retrieves the relevant chunks.

2.6 What Is an API?

API stands for Application Programming Interface.

An API lets one software program communicate with another.

In this book, your Python program communicates with an AI provider.

The flow looks like this:

Your Python app
↓
API request
↓
AI provider
↓
Model response
↓
Your Python app

You send a request with:

  • API key
  • Model name
  • Prompt
  • Settings

The provider returns a response.

OpenAI’s current Python quickstart shows a basic Python API call using the official SDK, the OpenAI client, the Responses API, and response.output_text for retrieving text output. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}

2.7 Why Use a Reusable Client?

In Chapter 1, the API call lived directly inside the project.

That is fine once.

But later, you will build many apps:

  • Command-line assistant
  • RAG assistant
  • Tool agent
  • Memory assistant
  • Workflow agent
  • Research agent
  • Guarded assistant
  • Evaluation runner
  • Deployed capstone app

You do not want to rewrite the same API code in every project.

A reusable client gives you one interface:

client.complete(system=system_prompt, user=user_prompt)

That makes your app cleaner.

It also makes future changes easier.

If you switch model names, add logging, add retries, or adapt to another provider, you can update one client instead of many files.

2.8 Model Selection

Different models can have different strengths.

Some may be:

  • Faster
  • Cheaper
  • Better at reasoning
  • Better at coding
  • Better at following structured formats
  • Better at long context
  • Better for tool calling

For beginner projects, choose a model that is:

  • Available to you
  • Cost-effective
  • Good enough for learning
  • Supported by your provider’s current SDK

This book uses a model name in .env so you can change it later:

OPENAI_MODEL=gpt-4.1-mini

Model names, pricing, capabilities, and API behavior can change over time.

Before publishing or deploying a serious app, check your provider’s current documentation.

2.9 Temperature

Temperature is a setting that affects randomness.

Lower temperature usually gives more consistent responses.

Higher temperature usually gives more varied responses.

For technical apps, lower is usually better.

Example:

OPENAI_TEMPERATURE=0.2

Use lower temperature for:

  • Code explanation
  • RAG answers
  • Structured output
  • Data extraction
  • Business workflows
  • Evaluation-sensitive apps

Use higher temperature carefully for:

  • Brainstorming
  • Creative writing
  • Naming ideas
  • Marketing drafts

For most projects in this book, a temperature around 0.2 is a good learning default.

2.10 Cost Awareness

AI APIs usually cost money based on usage.

Usage often depends on:

input tokens
+ output tokens
+ model choice
+ number of calls

A simple assistant might make one model call.

A multi-agent workflow might make five calls.

A RAG app might send long document context.

A tool-using agent might call the model to choose a tool, run the tool, and call the model again to explain the result.

Cost control matters.

Beginner cost-control habits:

Use concise prompts.
Avoid unnecessary model calls.
Test non-API code without calling the model.
Use small examples while developing.
Retrieve only relevant context.
Do not send full documents unless needed.
Track calls in serious projects.

You will build a simple cost-estimation system in Chapter 11.

2.11 Provider Adaptability

This book uses OpenAI-style examples because they are easy to demonstrate with Python.

But the architecture should not lock you into one provider forever.

A good AI app separates:

Application logic
from
Provider-specific API logic

That means your app should call:

client.complete(system, user)

instead of directly calling provider APIs everywhere.

Later, you could create:

OpenAIClient
AnthropicClient
LocalModelClient
MockClient

with the same basic interface.

That is professional design.

2.12 Project: Reusable Python LLM Client

What This Project Does

This project creates a reusable Python class for calling an LLM.

It will:

  1. Read configuration from environment variables
  2. Check that an API key exists
  3. Build a model input from system and user text
  4. Send the request to the provider
  5. Return text output
  6. Provide a mock client for tests and examples
  7. Include tests for non-API logic

Who This Helps

This project helps:

  • Python learners
  • AI app builders
  • Students creating portfolio projects
  • Freelancers building reusable tools
  • Developers who want cleaner code

What You Will Build

Create this project structure:

chapter_02_llm_client/
.env.example
.gitignore
requirements.txt
llm_client.py
demo.py
test_llm_client.py
README.md

2.13 Setup

Step 1: Create the Folder

mkdir chapter_02_llm_client
cd chapter_02_llm_client

Step 2: Create a Virtual Environment

python -m venv .venv

Activate it.

On macOS or Linux:

source .venv/bin/activate

On Windows PowerShell:

.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

Step 3: Create requirements.txt

openai
python-dotenv
pytest

Install dependencies:

pip install -r requirements.txt

Step 4: Create .env.example

OPENAI_API_KEY=replace_with_your_api_key
OPENAI_MODEL=gpt-4.1-mini
OPENAI_TEMPERATURE=0.2

Copy it to .env.

On macOS or Linux:

cp .env.example .env

On Windows PowerShell:

Copy-Item .env.example .env

Then edit .env and add your real API key.

Never publish your real .env file.

2.14 File: .gitignore

Create .gitignore:

.env
.venv/
__pycache__/
.pytest_cache/
*.pyc
*.log

This keeps secrets and local files out of version control.

2.15 File: llm_client.py

Create llm_client.py:

"""
Chapter 2 Project: Reusable Python LLM Client

This module provides a small reusable client for calling an LLM API.

Security notes:
- Never hardcode API keys.
- Store API keys in environment variables.
- Do not commit .env files.
"""

import os
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Protocol
from dotenv import load_dotenv
from openai import OpenAI

load_dotenv()

def get_env_float(name: str, default: float) -> float:
"""
Read a float from an environment variable.

If the variable is missing or invalid, return the default.
"""

raw_value = os.getenv(name)

if raw_value is None:
return default

try:
 return float(raw_value)
 except ValueError:
 return default

@dataclass
class LLMConfig:
"""Configuration for the LLM client."""

model: str = field(
 default_factory=lambda: os.getenv("OPENAI_MODEL", "gpt-4.1-mini")
 )
 temperature: float = field(
 default_factory=lambda: get_env_float("OPENAI_TEMPERATURE", 0.2)
 )

class LLMProvider(Protocol):
"""
Protocol for LLM clients.

Any provider class with a complete(system, user) method can follow this interface.
"""

def complete(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
"""Return model-generated text."""
...

class LLMClient:
"""
Reusable client for sending prompts to an LLM.

This implementation uses the OpenAI Python SDK.
The rest of your app should depend on complete(), not provider-specific details.
"""

def __init__(self, config: LLMConfig | None = None):
 self.config = config or LLMConfig()
 api_key = os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY")

if not api_key:
raise ValueError(
"OPENAI_API_KEY is missing. Add it to your .env file."
)

self.client = OpenAI(api_key=api_key)

def build_input(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
"""
Combine system and user instructions into readable model input.
"""

if not system.strip():
 raise ValueError("System instruction cannot be empty.")
if not user.strip():
 raise ValueError("User request cannot be empty.")

return f"""
System instruction:
{system.strip()}

User request:
{user.strip()}
"""

def complete(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
"""
Send a request to the model and return text output.
"""

model_input = self.build_input(system=system, user=user)

response = self.client.responses.create(
model=self.config.model,
input=model_input,
temperature=self.config.temperature,
)

return response.output_text

class MockLLMClient:
"""
Mock client for tests and examples.

This avoids live API calls when you only need predictable output.
"""

def __init__(self, response_text: str = "Mock response"):
 self.response_text = response_text
 self.calls: list[dict[str, str]] = []

def complete(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
"""
Return a fixed response and record the call.
"""

if not system.strip():
 raise ValueError("System instruction cannot be empty.")
if not user.strip():
 raise ValueError("User request cannot be empty.")

self.calls.append(
{
"system": system,
"user": user,
}
)

return self.response_text

Not executed automatically: requires live API credentials, network access, or external service.

The current OpenAI Python reference describes the Responses API as the primary API for interacting with models and shows response.output_text as a convenience for text output. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}

2.16 File: demo.py

Create demo.py:

"""
Demo script for the reusable LLM client.
"""

from llm_client import LLMClient

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """
You are a helpful Python tutor.

Explain concepts clearly for beginner-to-intermediate learners.
Be concise and practical.
Do not invent facts.
"""

def main() -> None:
"""Run a simple demo."""

client = LLMClient()

user_question = "Explain Python dictionaries in one paragraph with a simple example."

response = client.complete(
system=SYSTEM_PROMPT,
user=user_question,
)

print(response)

if __name__ == "__main__":
main()

Test result: Python syntax check passed.

This is intentionally small.

The goal is to prove that the client works.

2.17 File: test_llm_client.py

These tests check non-API logic.

They do not call the live model.

import pytest

from llm_client import (
LLMConfig,
MockLLMClient,
get_env_float,
)

def test_get_env_float_returns_default_when_missing(monkeypatch):
monkeypatch.delenv("TEST_FLOAT", raising=False)

result = get_env_float("TEST_FLOAT", 0.2)

assert result == 0.2

def test_get_env_float_returns_default_when_invalid(monkeypatch):
monkeypatch.setenv("TEST_FLOAT", "not-a-number")

result = get_env_float("TEST_FLOAT", 0.2)

assert result == 0.2

def test_get_env_float_reads_valid_value(monkeypatch):
monkeypatch.setenv("TEST_FLOAT", "0.7")

result = get_env_float("TEST_FLOAT", 0.2)

assert result == 0.7

def test_llm_config_can_be_created():
 config = LLMConfig(model="test-model", temperature=0.1)
assert config.model == "test-model"
 assert config.temperature == 0.1
def test_mock_client_returns_response():
 client = MockLLMClient(response_text="Hello from mock")

response = client.complete(
system="You are helpful.",
user="Say hello.",
)

assert response == "Hello from mock"

def test_mock_client_records_calls():
 client = MockLLMClient(response_text="Mock response")

client.complete(
system="System prompt",
user="User prompt",
)

assert len(client.calls) == 1
 assert client.calls[0]["system"] == "System prompt"
 assert client.calls[0]["user"] == "User prompt"
def test_mock_client_rejects_empty_system():
 client = MockLLMClient()

with pytest.raises(ValueError):
client.complete(system=" ", user="Hello")

def test_mock_client_rejects_empty_user():
 client = MockLLMClient()

with pytest.raises(ValueError):
client.complete(system="You are helpful.", user=" ")

2.18 File: README.md

Create README.md:

## Project: Reusable Python LLM Client

This project creates a reusable Python client for calling an LLM API.

## Features

- Reads API key from environment variables
- Reads model name from environment variables
- Reads temperature from environment variables
- Provides a clean `complete(system, user)` method
- Includes a mock client for tests
- Includes non-API unit tests

## Setup

python -m venv .venv

source .venv/bin/activate

pip install -r requirements.txt

cp .env.example .env

On Windows PowerShell:

python -m venv .venv

.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

pip install -r requirements.txt

Copy-Item .env.example .env

Edit `.env` and add your API key.

## Run Tests

pytest

## Run Demo

python demo.py

## Environment Variables

OPENAI_API_KEY=your_api_key OPENAI_MODEL=gpt-4.1-mini OPENAI_TEMPERATURE=0.2

## Notes

- Never commit `.env`.
- Model names and pricing may change.
- The mock client lets you test app logic without live API calls.
- You can adapt this pattern to other providers by creating another class with the same `complete(system, user)` method.

2.19 How the Code Works

This project has four important parts.

Part 1: Configuration

The LLMConfig class stores model settings.

@dataclass
class LLMConfig:
model: str
temperature: float

The model and temperature are loaded from environment variables.

That means you can change:

OPENAI_MODEL
OPENAI_TEMPERATURE

without editing Python code.

Part 2: Provider Interface

The LLMProvider protocol describes a simple interface:

def complete(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
...

This is useful because your app can depend on a simple behavior rather than a specific provider.

Later, you could create another class that follows the same interface.

Part 3: Real Client

The LLMClient class calls the live API.

It checks that the API key exists.

It builds the input.

It sends the request.

It returns text.

Your app does not need to know the provider details.

Part 4: Mock Client

The MockLLMClient class returns a fixed response.

This is useful for tests.

Instead of spending credits or waiting for network calls, you can test your app logic with predictable output.

2.20 Sample Usage

Once your .env file is configured, this code:

from llm_client import LLMClient

client = LLMClient()

response = client.complete(
system="You are a helpful Python tutor.",
user="Explain Python dictionaries in one paragraph.",
)

print(response)

might return:

A Python dictionary is a collection that stores data as key-value pairs. Each key is used to look up its associated value. For example, {"name": "Asha", "age": 25} stores a name and an age that can be accessed using their keys.

This is sample output only.

Do not claim exact output unless you run the code and capture the real result.

2.21 Testing the Project

Run:

pytest

Expected type of result:

8 passed

The exact timing may vary.

These tests do not call the live model API.

They check:

  • Environment float parsing
  • Configuration creation
  • Mock client output
  • Mock client call recording
  • Empty input validation

This is a good development habit.

You should not need a live API call to test basic Python logic.

2.22 Live API Testing

After adding your API key to .env, run:

python demo.py

The demo should print an explanation of Python dictionaries.

If you see:

OPENAI_API_KEY is missing

then your .env file is missing or not loaded.

Check:

.env exists
OPENAI_API_KEY is spelled correctly
python-dotenv is installed
you are running the command from the project folder

2.23 Why This Client Will Help Later

In the next chapter, you will build a command-line AI assistant.

That assistant will need to call the model for different commands:

/ask
/explain
/summarize
/tasks

Without a reusable client, every command might repeat API code.

With the client, each command can simply call:

client.complete(system=system_prompt, user=user_prompt)

Later chapters will use the same idea for:

  • RAG answers
  • Tool routers
  • Memory-powered assistants
  • Workflow agents
  • Reviewers
  • Evaluation scripts
  • Deployed apps

This is the point of reusable code.

You build it once, then benefit many times.

2.24 Provider-Agnostic Thinking

Even though this chapter uses one provider-style implementation, the design is flexible.

Your app should not care whether the response comes from:

OpenAI
Anthropic
local model
mock client
future provider

Your app should care that the object has:

complete(system, user)

That means you can later create:

class AnthropicClient:
 def complete(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
 ...

or:

class LocalModelClient:
 def complete(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
 ...

or:

class MockLLMClient:
 def complete(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
 return "Mock response"

This design makes your code more adaptable.

2.25 Common API Errors

Error 1: Missing API Key

Cause:

OPENAI_API_KEY is not set.

Fix:

Create .env and add your key.

Error 2: Wrong Model Name

Cause:

The model name is unavailable or misspelled.

Fix:

Check your provider’s current model list.

Error 3: Package Not Installed

Cause:

openai or python-dotenv is missing.

Fix:

pip install -r requirements.txt

Error 4: Running From the Wrong Folder

Cause:

.env is in the project folder, but you are running Python elsewhere.

Fix:

cd chapter_02_llm_client
python demo.py

Error 5: Expecting Exact Same Output Every Time

Model output can vary.

Even with low temperature, wording may change.

Test meaning and structure, not always exact strings.

2.26 Cost-Saving Development Pattern

Use this pattern while building AI apps:

1. Write prompt builder functions.
2. Test prompt builder functions without API calls.
3. Use a mock client for app logic.
4. Run live API tests only after normal logic works.
5. Capture real outputs only when preparing final publication.

This pattern saves credits.

It also makes debugging easier.

If your app logic is broken, do not blame the model first.

Test the normal Python parts.

2.27 Real-World Use Case

A reusable LLM client is useful in any serious AI project.

For example, a freelance automation app might need:

analyze_client_message()
draft_proposal()
draft_followup_email()
review_output()

Each function can use the same client.

A document assistant might need:

answer_question_from_context()
summarize_document()
generate_followup_questions()

Again, one client.

A multi-agent workflow might need:

planner_agent()
researcher_agent()
writer_agent()
reviewer_agent()

Again, one client.

Reusable infrastructure makes AI projects easier to maintain.

2.28 Monetization and Portfolio Angle

You can present this project as:

Reusable Python LLM Client

Portfolio description:

A clean Python wrapper for calling an LLM API using environment-based configuration, safe API-key handling, structured system/user prompts, and a mock client for testing.

This project is not flashy by itself.

But it shows maturity.

A beginner shows a chatbot.

A stronger developer shows reusable architecture.

Clients and employers value people who can build maintainable systems.

2.29 Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Copying API Calls Everywhere

Repeated API code becomes hard to update.

Use a reusable client.

Mistake 2: Hardcoding Secrets

Never write real API keys into Python files.

Mistake 3: Not Separating System and User Prompts

Keep stable assistant behavior separate from changing user requests.

Mistake 4: Testing Everything With Live API Calls

Use mock clients and unit tests for normal Python logic.

Mistake 5: Ignoring Cost

Every model call can cost money.

Avoid unnecessary calls.

Mistake 6: Locking Your App Too Tightly to One Provider

Wrap provider-specific details behind your own interface.

Mistake 7: Assuming API Behavior Never Changes

AI APIs evolve.

Keep provider-specific code isolated and check current documentation before serious deployment.

2.30 Best Practices

Use a .env file for local secrets.

Never commit .env.

Keep API code in one reusable client.

Use system prompts for assistant behavior.

Use user prompts for the current request.

Validate empty inputs.

Use mock clients for tests.

Keep model names configurable.

Use lower temperature for technical tasks.

Track model calls in serious apps.

Document setup steps clearly.

2.31 Mini Challenges

Challenge 1: Add a max_chars Input Check

Modify LLMClient.build_input() to reject very long user input.

Example:

if len(user) > 6000:
raise ValueError("User request is too long.")

Challenge 2: Add Basic Logging

Log every call to:

llm_calls.log

Include:

timestamp
model
input character count

Do not log secrets or sensitive user data.

Challenge 3: Add a complete_safe() Method

Create a method that catches errors and returns a friendly message instead of raising.

Example:

def complete_safe(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
 try:
 return self.complete(system, user)
 except Exception as error:
 return f"LLM error: {error}"

Challenge 4: Add a Local Mock Demo

Create:

mock_demo.py

Use MockLLMClient to simulate a response without an API key.

Challenge 5: Add Provider Notes

Add a PROVIDER_NOTES.md file explaining how another provider could be added using the same complete(system, user) interface.

2.32 Chapter Summary

In this chapter, you learned the practical foundation of LLM-powered Python apps.

You learned what LLMs, prompts, tokens, context, APIs, models, temperature, and cost mean in application development.

You also built a reusable Python LLM client.

This client gives you a clean interface:

client.complete(system, user)

That small design choice will make every future project easier.

In Chapter 1, you built a simple assistant.

In Chapter 2, you built reusable infrastructure.

In Chapter 3, you will use that infrastructure to create your first command-line AI application.

Key Takeaways

  • An LLM is one part of an AI application, not the whole app.
  • A prompt is a clear instruction sent to the model.
  • System instructions define assistant behavior.
  • User requests define the current task.
  • Tokens affect cost, speed, and context length.
  • APIs let your Python app communicate with AI providers.
  • A reusable LLM client prevents duplicated API code.
  • Mock clients help you test without live API calls.
  • Keep provider-specific details isolated.
  • Model names, pricing, and API behavior can change, so design for adaptability.
